source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 24 (PDF 215-227, printed 215-227); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 24 (Evolution), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 Evolution is the gradual change, over successive generations, in a population's:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.1: evolution is the gradual change in the genetic makeup (allele frequencies) of a population, which may form new species.

book_ref.quote: Evolution is the gradual change in the genetic makeup (allele frequencies) of a population

blocks.prompt: 2 Which was one of the earliest speculations of the concept of evolution?

options.text: Today's organisms were not created at once
Organisms always existed in their present form
Living things arise from non-living matter

blocks.explanation: Section 24.1: the speculations were that the universe and organisms did not always exist in present form, were not created at once, and resulted from changes from lower to higher forms.

book_ref.quote: They are the result of innumerable changes from the lower to the higher form

blocks.prompt: 3 Natural selection results in:

options.text: an increase in the percentage of individuals with better traits

blocks.explanation: Section 24.1: organisms with beneficial traits produce next generations, so individuals with better traits increase in percentage.

book_ref.quote: It results in the increase in the percentage of individuals with better traits in populations

blocks.prompt: 4 The 'theory of intelligent design' is another name for:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.1 (box): creationism says all organisms were created as they exist today, each individually, without change.

book_ref.quote: According to the theory of Creationism (“theory of intelligent design”)

blocks.prompt: 5 The early belief that living creatures can develop from non-living matter is called:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.1 (box): experiments disproved spontaneous generation, but could not negate creationism.

book_ref.quote: It was called idea of spontaneous generation

blocks.prompt: 6 Darwin travelled as a naturalist on HMS Beagle in:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2: in 1831 he travelled on HMS Beagle on a 5-year voyage around the world.

book_ref.quote: In 1831, he travelled as a naturalist on scientific expedition

blocks.prompt: 7 The voyage of HMS Beagle around the world lasted:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2: Darwin made a 5-year voyage around the world.

book_ref.quote: He made a 5-year voyage around the world

blocks.prompt: 8 Darwin's discovery of fossils of gigantic extinct mammals suggested that:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2: organisms looked very different in the past, suggesting that living things change over time.

book_ref.quote: He dug up fossils of gigantic extinct mammals

blocks.prompt: 9 On the Galápagos Islands Darwin saw that giant tortoises of different islands differed in:

options.text: the shape of their shells (saddle-shaped or dome-shaped)

blocks.explanation: Section 24.2: tortoises on one island had saddle-shaped shells, on another dome-shaped shells.

book_ref.quote: the giant tortoises on one island had saddle-shaped shells

blocks.prompt: 10 Many Galápagos plants and animals resembled most closely those of:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2: many resembled the plants and animals of South America rather than those of other islands.

book_ref.quote: many plants and animals resembled more with the plants and animals of South America

blocks.prompt: 11 The different sizes and shapes of beaks of Galápagos finches were:

options.text: adaptations for feeding on different kinds of food

blocks.explanation: Section 24.2: the beak differences were adaptations for feeding on different kinds of food on different islands.

book_ref.quote: differences in the sizes and shapes of beaks were actually adaptations for feeding

blocks.prompt: 12 Darwin thought a new species would arise from an ancestral form by:

options.text: gradual accumulation of adaptations to a different environment

blocks.explanation: Section 24.2: by gradual accumulation of adaptations to a different environment, separated from the original habitat.

book_ref.quote: A new species would arise from an ancestral form by the gradual accumulation of adaptations

blocks.prompt: 13 Darwin published 'On the Origin of Species' in:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.1: Darwin (1809-1882) published the book in 1859.

book_ref.quote: In 1859, he published his book “On the Origin of Species”

blocks.prompt: 14 Darwin's point of overproduction is illustrated in the book by a female sea star that releases each season about:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.1: a female sea star releases about 1 million eggs each season; organisms have far greater reproductive potential than is realized.

book_ref.quote: a female sea star releases about 1 million eggs each season

blocks.prompt: 15 Which statement about variations in Darwin's theory is correct?

options.text: Any two individuals are usually exactly alike
Inherited variations can be passed on to offspring
Variations are produced by the wish of organisms

blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.1: seldom are any two individuals exactly alike; variations may be advantageous, harmful or neutral; inherited variations pass to offspring.

book_ref.quote: Inherited variations can be passed on to offspring

blocks.prompt: 16 A neutral variation is one that is:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.1: variations may be advantageous, harmful or neutral (neither helpful nor harmful).

book_ref.quote: neutral (neither helpful nor harmful)

blocks.prompt: 17 Variations that keep individuals successful in reproduction during the struggle for survival are called:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.1: individuals with advantageous variations remain successful in reproduction; these are adaptive traits.

book_ref.quote: Such variations are called adaptive traits

blocks.prompt: 18 Disadvantageous traits in a population, over generations:

options.text: become less frequent and are eventually eliminated

blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.1: organisms with disadvantageous traits are less likely to reproduce, so such traits become rare and are eliminated.

book_ref.quote: such traits become less frequent in a population and eventually are eliminated

blocks.prompt: 19 Darwin's and Wallace's theories were presented together to the Linnean Society in:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.1 (box): both theories were presented in 1858; Wallace's letter was also of 1858 (the printed 1957 is a misprint).

book_ref.quote: When both Darwin’s and Wallace’s theories were presented to the Linnaean Society in 1858

blocks.prompt: 20 Neo-Darwinism was developed by integrating Darwinism with:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.2: in the early 20th century Darwinism was integrated with modern genetics.

book_ref.quote: the Darwinism was integrated with modern genetics to develop Neo-Darwinism

blocks.prompt: 21 Neo-Darwinism is based on the:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.2: Neo-Darwinism is based on the Hardy-Weinberg theorem and defines evolution as a change in allele frequency.

book_ref.quote: Neo-Darwinism is based on Hardy-Weinberg Theorem

blocks.prompt: 22 The Hardy-Weinberg theorem was presented in 1908 by Godfrey Hardy, an English mathematician, and Wilhelm Weinberg, a German:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.2: Wilhelm Weinberg was a German physician.

book_ref.quote: In 1908, English mathematician Godfrey Hardy and German physician Wilhelm Weinberg

blocks.prompt: 23 According to the Hardy-Weinberg theorem, in a large randomly mating population with no evolutionary forces, allele and genotype frequencies:

options.text: remain constant from generation to generation

blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.2: they remain constant if no evolutionary forces are acting.

book_ref.quote: remain constant from generation to generation, if no evolutionary forces are acting

blocks.prompt: 24 Random mating, a Hardy-Weinberg condition, means that:

options.text: every individual has an equal chance of mating with any other

blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.2: every individual must have an equal chance of mating with any other individual.

book_ref.quote: Every individual must have an equal chance of mating with any other individual

blocks.prompt: 25 If 600 out of 1000 genes for flower colour in a population are for red colour, the allele frequency of red is:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.2 (box): allele frequency = 600 ÷ 1000 = 0.6 (60%).

book_ref.quote: Gene pool means the total number of all genes for a trait in a population

blocks.prompt: 26 The number or proportion of individuals with a particular genotype in a population is the:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.2 (box): e.g., 40 RR plants out of 100 give a genotype frequency of 0.4.

book_ref.quote: Genotype frequency is the number or proportion of individuals with a particular genotype

blocks.prompt: 27 Genetic drift is often called:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.2: genetic drift, change by chance rather than fitness, is often called neutral selection.

book_ref.quote: Genetic drift is often called neutral selection

blocks.prompt: 28 Genetic drift is most obvious in:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.2: changes by chance are most obvious in small populations.

book_ref.quote: are most obvious in small populations

blocks.prompt: 29 A rabbit population reduced from 100 to 10 by a fire, whose survivors happen by chance to be mostly brown, will have:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.2: survival was by chance, not adaptation; the population has lower genetic diversity.

book_ref.quote: The resulting population will have lower genetic diversity

blocks.prompt: 30 The origin of all new genes is:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.2: mutations are the origin of all new genes and a source of variations.

book_ref.quote: Mutations, however, are a fact of life

blocks.prompt: 31 Mutational equilibrium exists when:

options.text: wild-type to mutant mutation is balanced by mutant to wild-type mutation

blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.2: balanced forward and back mutation has the same effect as no mutation; it rarely exists.

book_ref.quote: This has the same effect on allelic frequency as if no mutation occurred

blocks.prompt: 32 A measure of the tendency for gene frequencies to change through mutation is:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.2: this is mutation pressure.

book_ref.quote: Mutation pressure is a measure of the tendency for gene frequencies to change through mutation

blocks.prompt: 33 According to the book, most mutations are:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.2.2: most mutations are deleterious; some may be neutral or harmful in one environment and helpful in another.

book_ref.quote: Most are deleterious. Some may be neutral or harmful in one environment

blocks.prompt: 34 The study of the geographic distribution of plants and animals is:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.3.1: biogeography shows that life-forms in different parts of the world have distinctive evolutionary histories.

book_ref.quote: Biogeography (study of the geographic distribution of plants and animals)

blocks.prompt: 35 The major herbivores of Australia and Tasmania, cited as biogeographic evidence, are:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.3.1: organisms separated by barriers are often very different despite similar environments, e.g., kangaroos of Australia.

book_ref.quote: Many species of kangaroos are the major herbivores of Australia and Tasmania

blocks.prompt: 36 Islands often have relatively few but unique species because of:

options.text: island colonization and subsequent evolutionary events

blocks.explanation: Section 24.3.1: due to island colonization and subsequent evolutionary events.

book_ref.quote: Islands often have relatively few but unique species

blocks.prompt: 37 Body parts similar in structure but different in function are:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.3.2: these are homologous structures; the phenomenon is homology.

book_ref.quote: Body parts that are similar in structure but different in function are called homologous structures

blocks.prompt: 38 Homologous structures reveal:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.3.2: organisms with homologous structures have a common ancestor and evolved into different types.

book_ref.quote: Homologous structures reveal divergent evolution

blocks.prompt: 39 The wing of a bird and the wing of an insect are:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.3.2: both are adaptations for flight but not homologous; they are analogous organs showing convergent evolution.

book_ref.quote: The organs which are similar in function but differ in structure are called analogous organs

blocks.prompt: 40 The similarities between the wings of birds and insects simply reflect that, to fly, an animal must have:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.3.2: to fly, an animal must have a broad, flat gliding surface.

book_ref.quote: to fly, an animal must have a broad, flat gliding surface

blocks.prompt: 41 Minute remnants of hindlimb (pelvic) bones in pythons and boa constrictors are examples of:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.3.2: they are left over from appendages of reptilian ancestors, a clear indication of evolution.

book_ref.quote: some snakes like boa constrictors and pythons have minute remnants of hindlimb (pelvic) bones

blocks.prompt: 42 About how many vestigial structures are present in the human body, according to the book?
blocks.explanation: Section 24.3.2 (box): there are about 90, e.g., vermiform appendix, coccyx, wisdom teeth and ear muscles.

book_ref.quote: There are about 90 vestigial structures present in human body

blocks.prompt: 43 In humans, the vermiform appendix is a vestige of the:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.3.2 (box): the vermiform appendix is a vestige of the cecum; the coccyx is the remnant of the tail.

book_ref.quote: Vermiform appendix is a vestige of the cecum

blocks.prompt: 44 The wisdom teeth are vestigial third molars that human ancestors used for:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.3.2 (box): ancestors used them to help in grinding down plant tissue.

book_ref.quote: The wisdom teeth are vestigial third molars

blocks.prompt: 45 Molecular biology shows that, just as animals can have homologous structures, they may also have:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.3.3: related animals have similar DNA and similar proteins, i.e., homologous biochemicals.

book_ref.quote: they may also have homologous biochemicals

blocks.prompt: 46 Scientists estimate the time elapsed since evolution from a common ancestral molecule by comparing dissimilarities in DNA and proteins and assuming:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.3.3: by looking for dissimilarities in related proteins and DNA and assuming relatively constant mutation rates.

book_ref.quote: and by assuming relatively constant mutation rates

blocks.prompt: 47 A gene for antibiotic resistance in bacteria, according to the book, evolved by:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.3.3 (box): resistance may be due to mutations in bacterial genes; the gene evolved via natural selection and passes to next generations.

book_ref.quote: Antibiotic resistance means that bacteria are able to survive under the exposure of an antibiotic

blocks.prompt: 48 The earliest organisms on Earth, the prokaryotes, originated about:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.4: prokaryotes originated about 3.5 billion years ago; eukaryotes about 2 billion years ago.

book_ref.quote: originated in a very unstable environment from the reactions of organic molecules about 3.5 billion years ago

blocks.prompt: 49 Eukaryotes evolved from prokaryotes about:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.4: about 2 billion years ago.

book_ref.quote: About 2 billion years ago, eukaryotes evolved from prokaryotes

blocks.prompt: 50 The Endosymbiotic Theory was proposed by:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.4: Lynn Margulis proposed the Endosymbiotic Theory, the most acceptable theory for the evolution of eukaryotes.

book_ref.quote: This theory was proposed by Lynn Margulis

blocks.prompt: 51 According to the Endosymbiotic Theory, small engulfed prokaryotes able to do aerobic respiration became:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.4: aerobic small prokaryotes supplied energy to the large cell and became mitochondria.

book_ref.quote: Some of the small prokaryotes were able to do aerobic respiration

blocks.prompt: 52 Engulfed small cells that used sunlight to make food and shared it with the large cell became:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.4: they became the chloroplasts of eukaryotic cells.

book_ref.quote: Other small cells were able to use sunlight to make food

blocks.prompt: 53 Flagella of eukaryotes may have derived through the ingestion of prokaryotes similar to:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.4: flagella may have derived from ingested prokaryotes similar to spirochetes.

book_ref.quote: flagella may have derived through the ingestion of prokaryotes similar to spirochetes

blocks.prompt: 54 The DNA of mitochondria and chloroplasts is organized as:

options.text: a circular chromosome like that of prokaryotes

blocks.explanation: Section 24.4 (box): they have their own DNA organized in a circular chromosome like a prokaryotic chromosome.

book_ref.quote: Their DNA is organized in a circular chromosome like a prokaryotic chromosome

blocks.prompt: 55 Mitochondria and chloroplasts reproduce by:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.4 (box): they reproduce by binary fission like prokaryotes, whereas eukaryotic cells reproduce by mitosis.

book_ref.quote: Mitochondria (and chloroplasts) can reproduce by binary fission like prokaryotes

blocks.prompt: 56 According to the Membrane Invagination Theory, the nucleus and endoplasmic reticulum formed by:

options.text: infolding of the prokaryotic cell membrane into the cytoplasm

blocks.explanation: Section 24.4 (box): the cell membrane invaginated, giving rise to nucleus and ER and forming a eukaryotic cell (book correction).

book_ref.quote: the cell membrane of prokaryotic cell invaginated in the cytoplasm

blocks.prompt: 57 The power and efficiency of eukaryotic cells evolved by endosymbiosis enabled them to evolve:

options.text: multicellularity, cell specialization and large size

blocks.explanation: Section 24.4: they evolved multicellularity, cell specialization and large size, the key to the diversity of animals, plants and fungi.

book_ref.quote: Their power and efficiency enabled them to evolve new characteristics

blocks.prompt: 58 Jean-Baptiste Lamarck was a:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.5: Lamarck (1744-1829) was a French naturalist and an early proponent of evolution.

book_ref.quote: The French naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck (1744 - 1829)

blocks.prompt: 59 Lamarck presented his idea of progression in the book 'Philosophie Zoologique' (Zoological Philosophy), published in:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.5: published in 1809 (title corrected to 'Philosophie Zoologique').

book_ref.quote: In 1809, he published a book

blocks.prompt: 60 According to Lamarckism, organisms changed:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.5: organisms changed from simplest to complex as they adapted to the environment.

book_ref.quote: According to Lamarckism, organisms changed from simplest to complex

blocks.prompt: 61 Lamarck called changes in body parts caused by long-term use or disuse:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.5: he named them 'acquired characters'.

book_ref.quote: He named such changes in body parts, which occur due to long term use or disuse

blocks.prompt: 62 According to Lamarck's idea of use and disuse, organs that are used more frequently:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.5: organs used more develop and become strong; unused organs deteriorate.

book_ref.quote: the organs which are used more frequently are developed and become strong

blocks.prompt: 63 According to Lamarck's giraffe example, the short-necked ancestors of giraffe used to eat:

options.text: grass or leaves of small plants

blocks.explanation: Section 24.5: they ate grass or leaves of small plants; when these were unavailable they stretched their necks for tall trees.

book_ref.quote: They used to eat grass or the leaves of small plants

blocks.prompt: 64 In Lamarck's explanation, the longer neck gained by stretching during a giraffe's lifetime was:
blocks.explanation: Section 24.5: the strong, long neck gained in a lifetime was an acquired character, said to be inherited.

book_ref.quote: their necks became strong and long during their lifetime

blocks.prompt: 65 Lamarckism was disproved mainly because acquired characters:

options.text: have no genetic basis and cannot be inherited

blocks.explanation: Section 24.5.1: acquired characters have no genetic basis, so they cannot be inherited; organs are not modified by wish or need.

book_ref.quote: The acquired characters have no genetic basis
